blocks.text:
Design a Task Management System that lets users create tasks, declare dependencies between them ("this task cannot start until that one is done"), and pick the next task to work on. A task cannot be started while any of its dependencies are incomplete, and the system must reject any new dependency that would create a cycle in the dependency graph (a task indirectly depending on itself). When choosing what to work on next, the system picks the highest-priority task among those that are currently unblocked.

  • Actors: User (creates tasks, adds dependencies, starts and completes work), TaskManagementService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: a single workspace of tasks with a directed dependency graph, priority-based next-task selection, and status lifecycle tracking.

The distinguishing mechanic is graph-based: dependencies form a directed graph over tasks, and adding an edge requires a reachability check to detect and reject cycles, something no prior LLD problem in this set has needed.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Task creation: create a task with a title and a priority (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH), starting in TODO status.
Dependencies: declare that one task depends on another; the system rejects the dependency if it would create a cycle.
Starting work: a task can move to IN_PROGRESS only if every task it depends on is already DONE.
Completing work: an IN_PROGRESS task can be marked DONE.
Next task selection: among unblocked TODO tasks (all dependencies DONE), return the highest-priority one to work on next.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting many tasks and dependency edges must not require touching existing workflow logic.
Extensibility: a different next-task selection policy should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: prioritization, notification, and task creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: the cycle check is a graph traversal bounded by the number of tasks and edges, which stays small for a single workspace.
Thread safety: two requests starting the same task concurrently must not both succeed.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Can a task have multiple dependencies, or just one?
Should completing a task automatically unblock and notify dependents, or is that discovered lazily on the next startTask call?
Should removing a dependency be supported, in addition to adding one?
Is priority the only factor in next-task selection, or should task age or assignee workload also matter?
Should a task be allowed to depend on itself directly (a self-loop), or is that always rejected as a trivial cycle?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: A task may depend on any number of other tasks; the dependency graph is a general directed graph, not restricted to a tree.
Completing a task does not eagerly notify or unblock dependents; whether a task is unblocked is computed on demand, when startTask or getNextAvailableTask is called.
Removing a dependency once added is out of scope for this design.
A direct self-dependency (a task depending on itself) is treated as a cycle of length one and rejected by the same check as any longer cycle.

blocks.text: The design centers on three core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: Task, TaskStatus, TaskPriority, and dependency edges between tasks

items: Task: a unit of work with a title, priority, status, and a set of dependency task ids.
TaskStatus: an enum (TODO, IN_PROGRESS, DONE).
TaskPriority: an enum (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH).

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A task depends on many other tasks and is depended on by many tasks; every task has one status and one priority

items: Task to Task (depends on) is many-to-many, forming a directed graph.
Task to TaskStatus is one-to-one.
Task to TaskPriority is one-to-one.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep prioritization, notification, and task creation decoupled from the core service.

Why needed: how the "next task to work on" is chosen among unblocked tasks is a policy decision (highest priority first today, perhaps oldest-first or assignee-aware tomorrow) that changes independently of the dependency-tracking workflow.

Why it is the best fit: a new selection policy is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to TaskManagementService. What it solves: it isolates a frequently-revised planning policy from stable orchestration logic.
Why needed: task creation, dependency rejections, starts, blocks, and completions are all events a real project-tracking system would want to react to (activity feeds, notifications).

metadata.alt: TaskObserver interface notified by TaskManagementService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: TaskManagementService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core workflow from side effects.
Why needed: task id generation should not be scattered across calling code.
Why it is the best fit: creating tasks always goes through one consistent path. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: Task: attributes taskId, title, priority, status, dependencies; responsibility: represent one unit of work and its prerequisites.
TaskFactory: method createTask(title, priority); responsibility: generate sequential task ids.
TaskManagementService: the orchestrator; responsibility: manage the dependency graph, enforce the cycle check, gate task starts, select the next task, and notify observers.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: TaskPrioritizationStrategy and TaskObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: TaskPrioritizationStrategy: pickNext(unblockedTodoTasks): returns the task to work on next among the eligible candidates, or null if none are eligible.
TaskObserver: onTaskCreated / onDependencyRejected / onTaskStarted / onTaskBlocked / onTaskCompleted: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: The end-to-end workflows, alongside their rejection branches, look like this:

metadata.alt: Add dependency with cycle check, start task with completeness check, pick next task by priority

items: Dependency path: add dependency → reachability check finds no existing path back → edge added.
Cycle rejection path: add dependency → reachability check finds an existing path back → rejected.
Start path: start task → all dependencies DONE → mark IN_PROGRESS, or → an incomplete dependency exists → rejected as blocked.
Selection path: pick next task → filter to unblocked TODO tasks → choose the highest-priority one.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: createTask(title, priority): creates a new task in TODO status with no dependencies.
addDependency(taskId, dependsOnId): records that taskId depends on dependsOnId, or throws if that would create a cycle.
startTask(taskId): transitions a task to IN_PROGRESS if every dependency is DONE, or throws if blocked.
completeTask(taskId): transitions an IN_PROGRESS task to DONE.
getNextAvailableTask(): returns the highest-priority unblocked TODO task, or null if none qualify.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: DependencyCycleException: the requested dependency edge would create a cycle in the dependency graph.
TaskBlockedException: startTask is called while at least one dependency is not yet DONE.
InvalidTaskException: an unknown task id, or completeTask called on a task that is not IN_PROGRESS.

blocks.text: The critical race is two requests starting the exact same task at the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing to start the same task; synchronization ensures only one transitions it to IN_PROGRESS

blocks.text: Synchronizing the dependency-check-and-status-update step per task ensures the check and the transition happen atomically, so a task cannot be started twice.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new prioritization policy (oldest-first, assignee-aware) is a new TaskPrioritizationStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (activity feed, email digest) is a new TaskObserver implementation.
Eager unblocking (notifying dependents the moment a dependency completes) can be added inside completeTask without changing the public API.
Dependency removal can be added as a new service method, reusing the same reachability check in reverse to keep the graph consistent.
Single Responsibility: Task tracks state and its own dependency set, TaskPrioritizationStrategy decides ordering, TaskObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new prioritization or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to TaskManagementService.
Liskov Substitution: any TaskPrioritizationStrategy or TaskObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: TaskObserver exposes only the five lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: TaskManagementService depends on the TaskPrioritizationStrategy and TaskObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.
A task with zero dependencies is always eligible to start immediately.
A direct self-dependency (a task depending on itself) is caught by the same reachability check as a longer cycle and rejected.
getNextAvailableTask returns null when every TODO task has at least one incomplete dependency.
Completing a task that is not currently IN_PROGRESS (e.g., still TODO) throws InvalidTaskException.
addDependency: O(tasks plus edges) for the reachability check (a graph traversal from the prospective dependency back toward the task).
startTask: O(direct dependencies of the task) to check completeness.
getNextAvailableTask: O(tasks times average dependency count) to filter unblocked tasks, then O(unblocked tasks) to pick the highest priority.
Space: O(tasks plus dependency edges) held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: Task and a self-referencing TaskDependency join table

items: TaskDependency is a self-referencing join table on Task, recording each (taskId, dependsOnTaskId) edge.
An index on TaskDependency(dependsOnTaskId) speeds up the reachability traversal used by the cycle check.
Eagerly notify and re-evaluate dependents the moment a dependency completes, instead of only checking lazily on startTask.
Support dependency removal, reusing the reachability logic to keep the graph valid.
Add assignee-aware prioritization (e.g., balance workload across users) as an alternative TaskPrioritizationStrategy.
In a distributed deployment, move task-status locking to a database-level row lock or a distributed lock rather than in-process synchronization.

codes.python:
from enum import Enum

# Lifecycle status of a single task.
class TaskStatus(Enum):
    TODO = "TODO"                 # not started yet
    IN_PROGRESS = "IN_PROGRESS"  # currently being worked on
    DONE = "DONE"                  # finished

# How urgently a task should be worked on.
class TaskPriority(Enum):
    LOW = 1
    MEDIUM = 2
    HIGH = 3

# A single unit of work with its own dependency set.
class Task:
    def __init__(self, task_id, title, priority):
        self.task_id = task_id      # unique id, e.g. TASK-1
        self.title = title            # display title
        self.priority = priority      # urgency tier
        self.status = TaskStatus.TODO  # new tasks start as TODO
        self.dependencies = set()      # task ids that must be DONE first

    def add_dependency(self, depends_on_id):
        self.dependencies.add(depends_on_id)  # record a new dependency

# Creates tasks with sequential ids.
class TaskFactory:
    def __init__(self):
        self.counter = 0  # running id counter across all tasks created

    def create_task(self, title, priority):
        self.counter += 1  # bump id counter
        return Task(f"TASK-{self.counter}", title, priority)  # e.g. TASK-1

# Strategy interface: how the next task to work on is chosen.
class TaskPrioritizationStrategy:
    def pick_next(self, unblocked_todo_tasks):
        raise NotImplementedError  # returns the chosen task, or None if the candidate list is empty

# Picks the highest-priority candidate, breaking ties by lowest task id (earliest created).
class HighestPriorityFirstStrategy(TaskPrioritizationStrategy):
    def pick_next(self, unblocked_todo_tasks):
        best = None                                              # best candidate found so far
        for t in unblocked_todo_tasks:                              # scan all eligible tasks
            if (best is None
                    or t.priority.value > best.priority.value          # strictly higher priority wins
                    or (t.priority == best.priority and t.task_id < best.task_id)): # tie: earlier id wins
                best = t  # remember it
        return best  # the chosen task, or None if the list was empty

items: Why check reachability from dependsOnId back to taskId, rather than the other direction? Because the new edge is taskId depends-on dependsOnId; a cycle only forms if dependsOnId can already reach taskId through existing edges, closing the loop.

Why compute "unblocked" lazily instead of maintaining a live count of incomplete dependencies per task? Lazy computation is simpler to reason about and avoids keeping counters in sync across every dependency mutation, at the cost of a scan on every call.
How would you extend this to support removing a dependency? Simply remove the id from the dependency set; no cycle check is needed for removal since removing an edge can never create a cycle.

DFS reachability check on every addDependency call vs maintaining a topological order incrementally: the DFS check is simple and correct but costs O(tasks plus edges) per call; an incrementally maintained topological order (as used in some build systems) would make cycle checks faster at the cost of significantly more bookkeeping complexity.

Lazy unblocked-check vs eager dependent notification: lazy keeps completeTask simple (it does not need to know who depends on it), while eager notification could proactively alert dependents the moment they become unblocked, which is more responsive but more complex.
Priority-only next-task selection vs multi-factor scoring: priority alone is easy to reason about and test; a real system might blend in task age, assignee workload, or due dates.
Persist tasks and dependency edges in a relational database rather than in-memory maps, using the schema in the Database Design section.
Emit task lifecycle events to a message queue so downstream systems (activity feeds, notifications, analytics) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Add idempotency keys to createTask so retried network requests cannot create duplicate tasks.
Expose metrics on how often addDependency is rejected for cycles, which can reveal confusing or error-prone areas of a team's workflow.
